one_liner: Tencent's GPU-only C++17 2D renderer (PAG's engine), claimed 10-16x more animated rectangles per frame than Skia Ganesh m136.
what_it_does: TGFX is a lightweight 2D graphics library for GPUs that draws paths, rects, rounded rects, images and text, with optional SVG, PDF and layer-tree modules, on iOS, Android, HarmonyOS, macOS, Windows, Linux and the Web. Its API is Skia-shaped (Surface, Canvas, Paint, Path, Font, Image) but not source-compatible: you obtain a Device, call lockContext(), draw into a Surface's Canvas, then flush and submit the Context and unlock. It is the default rendering engine of PAG 4.0+ and is also used in Hippy and Tencent Docs per the README.
how_it_is_fast: OpsCompositor defers draws into pending lists and merges consecutive drawRect calls that share clip and brush (colour may differ and goes per vertex) into one RectDrawOp of up to RectDrawOp::MaxNumRects = 2048 rects, drawn with a cached shared index buffer (30 indices per coverage-AA quad). That turns the benchmark's 500k drawRect calls into a few hundred draw calls. With TGFX_USE_THREADS, which is on by default for native builds and the wasm-mt web build, vertex data is generated by async tasks on worker threads (RenderFlags::DisableAsyncTask turns this off for single-rect ops) into a shared, block-allocated vertex buffer. The rest of the speed is a small code base built for batching rather than Skia's general Ganesh op pipeline; V2.1 also added SIMD math (Highway is a dependency).
when_to_use: Animated 2D scenes with very many small, simple primitives (rects, rounded rects, sprites, atlas text) drawn on a GPU, where per-draw CPU overhead is the bottleneck.
Mobile or web apps that want a Skia-like API with a much smaller binary, especially on WebGL 2 or WebGPU via WebAssembly.
Projects already in the PAG/libpag ecosystem, or ones that need the same renderer on iOS, Android, HarmonyOS, desktop and the browser.
Layer-tree UIs with partial or tiled redraw (the V2.1 notes claim support for canvases of up to 200,000 layers).
when_not_to_use: Anything that needs a CPU or software rasterizer (headless servers, printing pipelines): TGFX is GPU-only, and Linux without a GPU needs SwiftShader. Blend2D, ThorVG's CPU backend or Skia's raster backend fit better there.

Workloads dominated by complex anti-aliased paths, strokes, gradients or blend modes: the only published comparison is the rectangle test, and the announcement says the platform runs only basic rectangle rendering.
When you need Skia's full feature set (SkSL runtime effects, Graphite, PDF/SVG fidelity, mature text shaping) or a drop-in Skia replacement.
When you need stable APIs: the latest tag is v2.1.1 (2025-09-26) while main has kept moving, and the benchmark repo itself needed a fix in August 2026 to adapt to the current TGFX window API.
Apple-only Metal deployments: the README still lists the Metal backend as in progress.

integration.form: static lib (CMake; dependencies synced with depsync)
integration.dependencies: pathkit and skcms (libpag forks), zlib, libpng, libwebp, libjpeg-turbo, FreeType, HarfBuzz, Highway, concurrentqueue; expat/json for SVG and PDF; shaderc, SPIRV-Cross, Vulkan-Headers, volk and VMA for Vulkan; Tint and Abseil for WebGPU (most codecs toggled by TGFX_USE_* options)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; Xcode 13+, GCC 9+, Visual Studio 2019+, CMake 3.13+, NDK 25 (25.2.9519653 recommended), Emscripten 4.0.15 pinned (4.0.11 rejected, 4.0.18+ breaks -sUSE_WEBGPU)
integration.platforms: iOS 15+, Android 5+, HarmonyOS 5+, macOS 12+, Windows 7+, Linux, Chrome 69+/Safari 15+; backends OpenGL 3.2+, OpenGL ES 3.0+, WebGL 2, Vulkan 1.1+, WebGPU, plus CMake options for D3D12 and Metal (README: Metal in progress)
integration.thread_safety: A Context may be used only between Device::lockContext() and unlock(); lockContext() blocks while another thread holds the device. Internal worker threads (TGFX_USE_THREADS) generate vertices and decode images.

gotchas: Batching is the speed source: a change of draw type, clip or brush (shader, filters, blend) flushes the pending batch, and a batch holds at most 2048 rects, so interleaved heterogeneous draws lose most of the advantage the rectangle benchmark shows.

The default web build is multithreaded wasm (pthreads with a worker pool of navigator.hardwareConcurrency); the README warns that renaming the generated .js breaks the worker bootstrap, and a single-threaded build (build:st) turns off async vertex generation.
Open correctness issue #1172 (January 2026): thin polygon strips render incorrectly. Earlier anti-aliasing seam (#1068) and Src/SrcIn path blend (#544) bugs are closed.

An independent user test in issue #381 (TGFX 1.2.1, Windows 11, December 2024) got about 30 FPS with 500 moving rects in TGFX versus about 100 FPS with 8,000+ in Skia. That predates the 2.0 rect batching and had no recorded maintainer resolution, but it is the only third-party data point found.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick TGFX over vkvg, vger or the Rive Renderer when you want a broad Skia-like GPU API that ships on mobile, desktop and the web (WebGL 2 and WebGPU) from one code base. Pick Blend2D, ThorVG (CPU) or Vello CPU when no GPU can be assumed or when you need independently measured numbers.
verified_claims_summary: The only number is first-party: discussion #567 (2025-04-24) reports 510,308 vs 34,721 animated 4-14 px anti-aliased rects held at 60 FPS (about 14.7x) for TGFX vs Skia chrome/m136 Ganesh, from the online WebGL benchmark built from libpag/tgfx-benchmark (TGFX main commit a56652e) and libpag/skia-benchmark. Device, GPU and browser are not stated. Reading the April 2025 harness code shows the two sides were not timed alike: Skia's frame time includes flushAndSubmit with GrSyncCpu::kYes (a blocking wait for the GPU), TGFX's flushAndSubmit() used syncCpu=false, and the ramp-and-stop rule keys on that frame time, so the 14.7x is inflated by an unknown amount.
status_note: Very active (last commit 2026-09-24, 1.6k stars, BSD-3-Clause, copyable), but the latest tagged release, v2.1.1, is a year behind main, and the only performance evidence is a first-party rectangle test whose harness favours TGFX.
measurement_flaws_found: Frame-time asymmetry in the web harness behind the quoted numbers: skia-benchmark web/demo/src/SkiaView.cpp at 7b5a2e9 (the m136 commit of 2025-04-08, unchanged on main) calls skContext->flushAndSubmit(skSurface.get(), static_cast<GrSyncCpu>(true)) before reading the clock, so Skia's measured draw time includes waiting for the GPU to finish. tgfx-benchmark web/demo/src/TGFXBaseView.cpp at 245ed1a (2025-04-07) calls context->flushAndSubmit(), whose syncCpu parameter defaults to false (include/tgfx/gpu/Context.h at v2.1.0). Since 2025-11-24 TGFX submits each frame's recording one frame late (lastRecording swap).

ParticleBench ramps the count while the measured draw time is under 16.7 ms and stops only when FPS < 59.5 AND the average draw time > about 14.7 ms. For Skia the draw time includes GPU execution, so it stops at the true GPU limit. For TGFX a GPU-bound frame can drop FPS while the CPU-only draw time stays under the threshold, so the count can keep climbing past the real 60-FPS point. The FPS shown in the announcement's screenshots could not be checked (private-user-images).
Build asymmetry: the Skia web harness links with -sASSERTIONS=2 (both at 7b5a2e9 and on main) while the TGFX harness does not. Its runtime cost was not measured.

Thread asymmetry: the default web build is wasm-mt, where TGFX_USE_THREADS moves rect vertex generation to worker threads (DataSource::Async already at the pinned TGFX commit a56652e). Skia's harness does all recording on the calling thread, so the test also compares a multithreaded renderer with a single-threaded one.
